danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 18
paragraphs: Da Pierre vendte hjem, blev han overrakt to af Rostoptjins proklamationer, der var kommet den dag.

Den første erklærede, at rygtet om, at grev Rostoptjin havde forbudt folk at forlade Moskva, var falskt; tværtimod var han glad for, at damer og handelskoner rejste. »Så bliver der mindre panik og mindre sladder,« stod der i proklamationen, »men jeg sætter mit liv som indsats på, at den slyngel ikke kommer ind i Moskva.« Disse ord viste tydeligt Pierre for første gang, at franskmændene ville indtage Moskva. Den anden proklamation meddelte, at hovedkvarteret var i Vjazma, at grev Wittgenstein havde besejret franskmændene, men at da mange af Moskvas indbyggere ønskede at bevæbne sig, var der våben klar til dem på arsenalet: sabler, pistoler og musketter, der kunne fås til en lav pris. Tonen i denne proklamation var ikke så spøgefuld som i de tidligere Tjigirin-samtaler. Pierre grundede over disse proklamationer. Den frygtelige uvejrssky, som han havde ønsket med hele sin sjæl, men som alligevel vakte ufrivillig rædsel i ham, nærmede sig tydeligvis.
»Skal jeg melde mig til hæren, eller skal jeg vente?« spurgte han sig selv for hundrede gang. Han tog et spil kort, der lå på bordet, og begyndte at lægge kabale.
»Hvis denne kabale går op,« sagde han til sig selv, efter at have blandet kortene og holde dem i hånden med løftet hoved, »hvis den går op, betyder det... hvad betyder det?«
Han havde endnu ikke afgjort, hvad det skulle betyde, da han hørte den ældste fyrstindes stemme ved døren, der spurgte, om hun måtte komme ind.
»Så betyder det, at jeg må drage i krig,« sagde Pierre for sig selv. »Kom ind, kom ind!« tilføjede han til fyrstinden.
Kun den ældste fyrstinde, hende med det stive ansigt og den lange talke, boede stadig i Pierres hus. De to yngre var begge blevet gift.

»Undskyld, at jeg forstyrrer Dem, fætter,« sagde hun med en bebrejdende og ophidset stemme. »Der må træffes en beslutning, det véd De. Hvad skal der ske? Alle har forladt Moskva, og folket gør oprør. Hvorfor bliver vi?«
»Tværtimod, forholdene synes tilfredsstillende, ma cousine,« sagde Pierre i den spøgende tone, han sædvanligvis anlagde over for hende, mens han altid følte sig utilpas i rollen som hendes velgører.

»Tilfredsstillende, sandelig! Meget tilfredsstillende! Barbara Ivanovna fortalte mig i dag, hvordan vores tropper udmærker sig. Det gør dem bestemt ære! Og folket er ganske oprørsk — selv min stuepige er begyndt at være uforskammet. I det tempo begynder de snart at slå os. Man kan ikke gå på gaden. Og oven i købet kan franskmændene være her når som helst, så hvad venter vi på? Jeg beder Dem kun om én ting, fætter,« fortsatte hun, »sørg for, at jeg bliver bragt til Petersborg. Hvad jeg end måtte være, kan jeg ikke leve under Bonapartes styre.«
»Åh, nu, ma cousine! Hvor har De Deres oplysninger fra? Tværtimod...«
»Jeg bøjer mig ikke for Deres Napoleon! Andre kan gøre, som de lyster.... Hvis De ikke vil gøre dette...«
»Men det vil jeg jo, jeg giver ordren med det samme.«
Fyrstinden var åbenbart ærgerlig over ikke at have nogen at være vred på. Hun mumlede noget for sig selv og satte sig i en stol.

»Men De er blevet misinformeret,« sagde Pierre. »Alt er roligt i byen, og der er ikke den mindste fare. Se her! Jeg har lige læst...« Han viste hende proklamationen. »Grev Rostoptjin skriver, at han sætter sit liv som indsats på, at fjenden ikke kommer ind i Moskva.«

»Åh, den greve!« sagde fyrstinden ondskabsfuldt. »Han er en hykler, en slyngel, som selv har ophidset folket til oprør. Stod der ikke i de der idiotiske proklamationer, at hvem som helst, 'uanset hvem det måtte være, skulle slæbes i håret til arresten'? (Hvor dumt!) 'Og ære og berømmelse til den, der fanger ham,' siger han. Det er, hvad hans smiger har ført os til! Barbara Ivanovna fortalte mig, at pøblen næsten slog hende ihjel, fordi hun sagde noget på fransk.«
»Åh, men nu tager De det hele for tungt,« sagde Pierre og begyndte at lægge kabale.

Selvom den kabale gik op, meldte Pierre sig ikke til hæren, men blev i det forladte Moskva i den samme tilstand af ophidselse, ubeslutsomhed og uro, men samtidig med glædelig forventning om noget forfærdeligt.

Næste dag mod aften rejste fyrstinden, og Pierres godsforvalter kom for at meddele ham, at pengene til udrustningen af hans regiment ikke kunne skaffes uden at sælge et af godserne. Generelt fik godsforvalteren det til at se ud, som om Pierres projekt med at opstille et regiment ville ruinere ham. Pierre lyttede til ham og kunne næppe undertrykke et smil.
»Nå, så sælg det,« sagde han. »Hvad skal man gøre? Jeg kan ikke trække mig nu!«

Jo værre alt gik, især hans egne affærer, jo mere tilfreds var Pierre, og jo tydeligere var det, at den katastrofe, han ventede, nærmede sig. Næsten ingen af hans bekendte var tilbage i byen. Julie var rejst, og det var fyrstinde Marja også. Af hans nære venner var kun familien Rostov tilbage, men han besøgte dem ikke.

For at adsprede sine tanker kørte han den dag til landsbyen Vorontsovo for at se den store ballon, som Leppich byggede til at tilintetgøre fjenden, og en prøveballon, der skulle stige næste dag. Ballonen var endnu ikke færdig, men Pierre erfarede, at den blev bygget på kejserens befaling. Kejseren havde skrevet til grev Rostoptjin som følger:
»Så snart Leppich er klar, saml en besætning af pålidelige og intelligente mænd til hans gondol og send en kurer til general Kutuzov for at underrette ham. Jeg har orienteret ham om sagen.«

»Indskærp over for Leppich at være meget forsigtig med, hvor han lander første gang, så han ikke begår en fejl og falder i fjendens hænder. Det er afgørende, at han koordinerer sine bevægelser med øverstbefalendes.«

På vej hjem fra Vorontsovo, da Pierre passerede Bolotnojetorvet og så en stor menneskemængde omkring Lobnojetorvet, standsede han og steg ud af sin vogn. En fransk kok, anklaget for at være spion, blev pisket. Piskningen var netop overstået, og bødlen var ved at løsne en kraftig mand med rødt skæg i blå strømper og en grøn jakke fra piskebænken; manden klagede sig ynkeligt. En anden fange, tynd og bleg, stod i nærheden. Ud fra deres ansigter var begge franskmænd. Med et skræmt og lidende udtryk, der lignede den tynde franskmands, pressede Pierre sig gennem mængden.
»Hvad er det? Hvem er det? Hvad er det for?« spurgte han uafladelig.

Men mængdens opmærksomhed — embedsmænd, borgere, handlende, bønder og kvinder i sjaler og pelsfrakker — var så ivrigt koncentreret om det, der foregik på Lobnojetorvet, at ingen svarede ham. Den kraftige mand rejste sig, rynkede panden, trak på skuldrene og forsøgte åbenbart at virke fattet, mens han trak i sin jakke uden at se sig omkring, men pludselig begyndte hans læber at skælve, og han brast i gråd, på den måde fuldblodige voksne mænd græder, selvom de er vrede på sig selv for det. Folk i mængden begyndte at tale højt, tilsyneladende for at dæmpe deres medlidenhed, syntes Pierre.
»Han er kok hos en eller anden fyrste.«
»Nå, monsieur, russisk sauce smager vist surt for en franskmand... sætter tænderne i stykker!« sagde en rynket kontorchef, der stod bag Pierre, da franskmanden begyndte at græde.
Kontorchefen så sig om i tydelig forventning om, at hans vittighed ville blive påskønnet. Nogle lo, andre vedblev at betragte bødlen med forfærdelse, mens han klædte den anden mand af.

Pierre gispede, hans ansigt forvrængedes, og han vendte sig hastigt om, gik tilbage til sin vogn og mumlede noget for sig selv, mens han satte sig ind. Mens de kørte, rystede han flere gange sammen og udbrød så højt, at kusken spurgte:
»Hvad behager?«
»Hvor kører du hen?« råbte Pierre til kusken, der kørte mod Lubjanka-gaden.
»Til guvernørens, som De befalede,« svarede kusken.
»Dumrian! Idiot!« råbte Pierre og skældte sin kusk ud — noget, han sjældent gjorde. »Hjem, sagde jeg! Og kør hurtigere, kvaj!« »Jeg må rejse herfra i dag,« mumlede han for sig selv.

Ved synet af den torturerede franskmand og mængden omkring Lobnojetorvet havde Pierre så definitivt bestemt sig for, at han ikke længere kunne blive i Moskva og ville rejse til hæren den selvsamme dag, at det syntes ham, at han enten havde sagt det til kusken, eller at manden burde have vidst det af sig selv.

Da Pierre nåede hjem, gav han ordre til Jevstafej — hans hovedkusk, der vidste alt, kunne alt og var kendt af hele Moskva — om, at han ville rejse den aften til hæren i Mozjajsk, og at hans rideheste skulle sendes derud. Dette kunne ikke ordnes den dag, så på Jevstafejs indvending måtte Pierre udskyde sin afrejse til næste dag for at give tid til at sende forspandshestene i forvejen.

Den fireogtyvende klarede vejret op efter regnvejr, og efter middag forlod Pierre Moskva. Da han skiftede heste den nat i Perkhusikovo, erfarede han, at der havde været et stort slag den aften. (Det var slaget ved Sjevardino.) Man fortalte ham, at der i Perkhusikovo rystede jorden af kanonilden, men ingen kunne svare på hans spørgsmål om, hvem der havde vundet. Ved daggry næste dag nærmede Pierre sig Mozjajsk.
Hvert hus i Mozjajsk var belagt med soldater, og på det herberg, hvor Pierre blev mødt af sin staldkarl og kusk, var der ingen plads. Det var fuldt af officerer.

Overalt i Mozjajsk og ud over det var tropper indkvarterede eller på march. Kosakker, fodfolk og ryttere, vogne, ammunitionskærrer og kanoner var overalt. Pierre pressede sig fremad så hurtigt, han kunne, og jo længere han kom fra Moskva og jo dybere han trængte ind i det hav af tropper, jo mere blev han grebet af en rastløs ophidselse og en ny og glædelig følelse, han ikke før havde oplevet. Det var en følelse beslægtet med den, han havde følt i Sloboda-paladset under kejserens besøg — en fornemmelse af nødvendigheden af at påtage sig noget og ofre noget. Han oplevede nu en glad bevidsthed om, at alt det, der udgør menneskets lykke — livets bekvemmeligheder, rigdom, ja selve livet — er noget ubetydeligt, som det er en glæde at kaste bort sammenlignet med noget... Med hvad? Pierre kunne ikke sige det, og han forsøgte ikke at afgøre, for hvem og for hvad han følte en sådan særlig fryd ved at ofre alt. Han var ikke optaget af spørgsmålet om, hvad han skulle ofre for; selve det at ofre skænkede ham en ny og glædelig fornemmelse.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: When Pierre returned home, he was handed two of Rostopchin's broadsheets that had been delivered that day.

The first declared that the report of Count Rostopchin forbidding people to leave Moscow was false; on the contrary, he was glad that ladies and merchants' wives were leaving the city. "There will be less panic and less gossip," the broadsheet read, "but I will stake my life that that scoundrel will not enter Moscow." These words showed Pierre clearly, for the first time, that the French would enter Moscow. The second broadsheet stated that Russian headquarters were at Vyazma, that Count Wittgenstein had defeated the French, but that since many Moscow residents wished to be armed, weapons were available at the arsenal: sabers, pistols, and muskets at a low price. The tone of the proclamation was not as playful as the earlier Chigirin bulletins. Pierre pondered these broadsheets. Clearly, the terrible storm he had longed for with his whole soul—yet which filled him with involuntary dread—was drawing near.
"Should I join the army and enlist, or wait?" he asked himself for the hundredth time. He took a pack of cards from the table and began laying them out for a game of patience.
"If this patience works out," he said to himself after shuffling the cards, holding them in his hand and looking up, "if it works out, it means... what does it mean?"
He hadn't decided what it would mean when he heard the eldest princess's voice at the door, asking whether she might come in.
"Then it will mean I must go to the army," Pierre said to himself. "Come in, come in!" he called to the princess.
Only the eldest princess—the one with the stony face and long waist—was still living in Pierre's house. The two younger ones had both married.

"Excuse me for disturbing you, cousin," she said in a reproachful, agitated voice. "But you know some decision must be made. What is going to happen? Everyone has left Moscow and the people are rioting. Why are we still here?"
"On the contrary, everything seems satisfactory, dear cousin," said Pierre in the bantering tone he habitually used with her, always feeling uncomfortable in the role of her benefactor.

"Satisfactory? Very satisfactory! Barbara Ivanovna was telling me today how our troops are distinguishing themselves. That is certainly to their credit! And the people too are getting quite unruly—even my maid has started being rude. At this rate they'll soon be beating us. One can't walk in the streets. But above all, the French will be here any day now, so what are we waiting for? I ask just one thing of you, cousin," she went on, "arrange for me to be taken to Petersburg. Whatever I may be, I can't live under Bonaparte's rule."
"Oh come, dear cousin! Where do you get your information? On the contrary..."
"I won't submit to your Napoleon! Others can if they wish... If you don't want to do this..."
"But I will, I'll arrange it right away."
The princess was clearly annoyed at having no one to be angry with. Muttering to herself, she sat down in a chair.

"But you've been misinformed," said Pierre. "Everything is quiet in the city and there's not the slightest danger. See—I was just reading..." He showed her the broadsheet. "Count Rostopchin writes that he'll stake his life that the enemy won't enter Moscow."

"Oh, that count of yours!" said the princess spitefully. "He's a hypocrite, a scoundrel who stirred up the people to riot himself. Didn't he write in those idiotic broadsheets that anyone, 'whoever it might be, should be dragged to the lockup by his hair'? How silly! 'And honor and glory to whoever catches him,' he says. That's what his flattery has led to! Barbara Ivanovna told me the crowd nearly killed her because she said something in French."
"Oh, but that's so... You take everything too much to heart," said Pierre, and began laying out his cards for patience.

Although the patience did come out, Pierre did not join the army but remained in the deserted city, still in the same state of agitation, indecision, and anxiety, yet at the same time joyfully awaiting something terrible.

The next day toward evening, the princess departed, and Pierre's chief steward came to inform him that the money needed to equip his regiment could not be found without selling one of the estates. The steward's general message was that Pierre's project of raising a regiment would ruin him. Pierre listened, barely suppressing a smile.
"Well then, sell it," he said. "What's to be done? I can't back out now!"

The worse everything became—especially his own affairs—the more pleased Pierre was, and the more evident it seemed that the catastrophe he expected was approaching. Almost no one he knew was left in town. Julie had gone, and Princess Mary too. Of his close friends, only the Rostovs remained, but he didn't go to see them.

To distract himself, he drove that day to the village of Vorontsovo to see the great balloon Leppich was building to destroy the enemy, and a trial balloon that was to go up the next day. The balloon wasn't ready yet, but Pierre learned it was being built by the Emperor's order. The Emperor had written to Count Rostopchin as follows:
As soon as Leppich is ready, assemble a crew of reliable and intelligent men for his gondola and send a courier to General Kutuzov to inform him. I have already told him about it.

Please impress upon Leppich that he must be very careful where he makes his first descent, so he doesn't make a mistake and fall into enemy hands. It is essential that he coordinate his movements with the commander in chief.

On his way home from Vorontsovo, passing through Bolotnaya Square, Pierre saw a large crowd around the Lobnoe Place and stopped to get out of his carriage. A French cook accused of being a spy was being flogged. The flogging had just ended, and the executioner was releasing from the flogging bench a stout man with red whiskers, wearing blue stockings and a green jacket, who was moaning piteously. Another man, thin and pale, stood nearby. Judging by their faces, both were French. With a frightened, suffering expression like the one on the thin Frenchman's face, Pierre pushed his way through the crowd.
"What is it? Who is it? What's it for?" he kept asking.

But the crowd—officials, townspeople, shopkeepers, peasants, and women in shawls and fur coats—was so absorbed in what was happening at the Lobnoe Place that no one answered him. The stout man got up, frowned, shrugged his shoulders, and clearly trying to look composed, began pulling on his jacket without looking around; but suddenly his lips trembled and he began to cry, the way full-blooded grown men cry, angry with themselves for doing so. People in the crowd began talking loudly, apparently to drown out their own feelings of pity, or so it seemed to Pierre.
"He's the cook to some prince."
"Well now, mister, seems Russian sauce is a bit sour for a Frenchman... sets his teeth on edge!" said a wrinkled clerk standing behind Pierre, as the Frenchman began to cry.
The clerk looked around, obviously hoping his joke would be appreciated. Some people laughed; others continued to watch in dismay as the executioner was undressing the other man.

Pierre choked, his face contorted, and he turned hastily away, went back to his carriage muttering something to himself, and climbed in. As they drove, he shuddered and cried out several times so loudly that the coachman asked:
"What is your pleasure?"
"Where are you going?" shouted Pierre to the coachman, who was heading toward Lubyanka Street.
"To the Governor's, as you ordered," answered the coachman.
"Fool! Idiot!" shouted Pierre, abusing his coachman—something he rarely did. "Home, I told you! And drive faster, you blockhead!" "I must get away this very day," he muttered to himself.

The sight of the tortured Frenchman and the crowd around the Lobnoe Place had so firmly decided Pierre that he could no longer stay in Moscow and would leave for the army that very day, that it seemed either he had already told the coachman this or that the man should have known it on his own.

On reaching home, Pierre ordered Evstafey—his head coachman, who knew everything, could do anything, and was known to all Moscow—to set out that night for the army at Mozhaysk, and to send his saddle horses ahead. This couldn't all be arranged that day, so on Evstafey's advice Pierre had to postpone his departure until the next day to allow time for the relay horses to go on ahead.

On the twenty-fourth, the weather cleared after a spell of rain, and after dinner Pierre left Moscow. When changing horses that night at Perkhushkovo, he learned that there had been a great battle that evening. (This was the battle of Shevardino.) He was told that there in Perkhushkovo the earth trembled from the gunfire, but nobody could answer his questions about who had won. At dawn the next day Pierre was approaching Mozhaysk.
Every house in Mozhaysk had soldiers quartered in it, and at the inn where Pierre was met by his groom and coachman there was no room to be had. It was full of officers.

Everywhere in Mozhaysk and beyond it, troops were stationed or on the march. Cossacks, infantry, cavalry, wagons, ammunition carts, and cannons were everywhere. Pierre pushed forward as fast as he could, and the farther he left Moscow behind and the deeper he plunged into that sea of troops, the more he was overcome by restless excitement and a new, joyful feeling he had never experienced before. It was a feeling similar to what he had felt at the Sloboda Palace during the Emperor's visit—a sense that he must undertake something and sacrifice something. He now experienced a glad awareness that everything that makes up human happiness—the comforts of life, wealth, even life itself—is rubbish that it is pleasant to throw away, compared with something... With what? Pierre could not say, and he didn't try to determine for whom or for what he felt such particular joy in sacrificing everything. He wasn't concerned with the question of what to sacrifice for; the very act of sacrificing brought him a new and joyful sensation.
